utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today is Thursday, the 13th of December, 2007. My greetings to Ms. Dahl, who represents the OTP. Good morning, Mr. Seselj. Good morning, Witness. And my morning greetings to all the people helping us out. Further to Rule 15 bis, Judge Lattanzi is absent this morning. She won't be sitting with us, because she has other commitments. Mr. Seselj, we have been doing our sums and you have 1 hour and 5 minutes, with an additional 20 minutes at your request, which means that you have until 10.30 to complete your cross-examination. This is what I wanted to tell you to start. And you -- without further ado, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Oberschall, yesterday afternoon or maybe last night did you talk to anyone about your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. The last question I asked you yesterday was about the attack on the Croatian civilian population in Vojvodina. Prior to that, you said that you are rather well informed, you had studied the problem. But then in your response you mentioned the report of Tadeusz Mazowiecki, who was an envoy of the UN Secretary-General. Is that correct? Do you remember that? That was the last thing.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, do you know that on several occasions I publicly condemned Tadeusz Mazowiecki as a liar and a cheat?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, he was not surprised either, because he knew he was a liar better than I did. Do you know that for --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I request an instruction to Mr. Seselj not to comment on the witness's answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the right to comment on the witness's answers because a new question follows up, and you cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. The witness said that he wasn't surprised when he answered, so I wondered, surprised at what? Because Mr. Mazowiecki would be a liar or surprised, because this was said by Mr. Seselj. So it was rather ambiguous. Witness, you said that you were not surprised. What did you mean exactly in saying so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what I meant is that -- I certainly didn't mean that former Polish Prime Minister, very distinguished person Mazowiecki was a liar, but I'm not surprised that Seselj -- Dr. Seselj calls a lot of people liars. Yesterday he called me a liar sitting right here. It's just sort of standard talk. You know, you don't like what somebody says; you call him a liar. I mean, he does that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I first have to observe that I did not call you a liar yesterday, Mr. Oberschall. I said you were lying. I didn't say you were a liar. The those are two very different things. If I said you were a liar, then you would have had the right to be offended, because I insulted you. But when I say that you are lying, you don't have the right to feel offended, because I have the right to say that here.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Improper cross-examination. This is not cross-examination, Your Honour. It's arguing with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do avoid arguing with the witness. Mr. Seselj, you believe that it may be that the witness lied. If that is so, say where, in which issues he lied, because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that yesterday in response to his claim that a research into 1992 Serbian media had been made showing that I was some kind of protege of the Serbian media. Let's not go into it. We're finished with that. But I never said that Mr. Oberschall was a liar. I never said that. And let him not put that into my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, do you know, since you read that report of Mazowiecki, that Mazowiecki in his report claims that I advocated deportation of Hungarians from Vojvodina, ethnic Hungarians. Did you read that in his report?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know by heart the specifics of these reports. Had I known that I would be questioned as an expert witness on the Mazowiecki reports rather than on your speeches, which I content analysed, I certainly could have brought these reports here with me and looked up what exactly Mr. Mazowiecki said. But the details or specifics, I can't recall here just -- just sitting here. No, I can't recall the specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, you do invoke Mr. Mazowiecki's report in your expert report, so you should have expected my questions about that report. It doesn't justify you, that you don't know the whole contents. But let's leave that aside. If what I just told you is correct --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You cannot stop me now. You cannot interrupt me. You will answer when I ask my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Give him time to put your question. I don't know what question is going to be raised, and you're already on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness was asking a question of the Chamber, and Mr. Seselj was talking over him and preventing him from interposing a request to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you want to say, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the -- Dr. Seselj alleges that I did not use the Mazowiecki material in my expert report, but I did actually. Dr -- Mazowiecki wrote a special report just on the media in -- during that time of 1992, 1993, and so on. And he -- his staff analysed the contents of the -- of the media, same as I, and that's -- I refer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing of interest to me - but I believe it is also of interest to the accused - is whether you, as an expert, you read that report. And you said you did. Very good.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to note again that the interpretation is disastrous, apparently. I said Mr. Oberschall used Mazowiecki's report in writing his expert report. They interpreted to him that he did not use the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, if it is correct that Mazowiecki's report claims that I publicly, through the media, advocated deportation of Hungarians from Vojvodina, and I never did that, was I then completely right in calling Mazowiecki a liar?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: The interpretation was correct. Mr. Seselj is talking too fast, not so much for the interpreters as for the court reporter. That's why it's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before -- before the witness answers, there's a note from the interpretation to the accused that you are talking too fast. That's why the interpreters have a difficulty in catching up with you. So if you would be kind enough to speak slower, that would then assist the interpreters. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj. It happened on several occasions that there are problems in interpretation. But it may be due to the speed of delivery, which may cause some problems. But here the question was crystal clear. There is no single problem. So please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Mazowiecki wrote, I think, about a dozen reports. They covered all of human rights violations in all of Yugoslavia, and in several of the reports there were special sections on Vojvodina. And we were talking yesterday about Vojvodina. And I think we still are talking today about Vojvodina. And he describes many human rights violations in connection with ethnic cleansing in the Vojvodina, intimidation of people, threats, beatings, evictions from houses, and so on. And that's what I've read. Specifically what Mazowiecki report says about you and what you said and didn't say, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, please instruct the witness to answer the question I directly asked. He is being evasive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If it is correct that Mazowiecki claims that I had advocated and asked for deportation of ethnic Hungarians, and I never did, was I right in publicly calling him a liar, if he is claiming something that is awful and is not true?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a -- it's a hypothetical. How do I know that what you say that Mazowiecki said about you is true or not. I have no way of checking that. If -- if I had some written statement by somebody other than you about what Mazowiecki said about you, then I could, you know, give an answer. But in this kind of hypothetical question, I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the result, the outcome of it for the Judges is as follows: You drew conclusions in your report based on what you could read in Mazowiecki's report, but in the event that Mr. Seselj is right when he says that with regard to the Hungarians in Vojvodina he never said anything, whilst it is stated in the report, could -- could such a thing have changed slightly or thoroughly some of your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, now you've gotten me totally confused about what I am -- what the question and what it's all about. I -- I just don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you don't understand, I'm going to put the question again. In this report it is alleged apparently that Mr. Seselj made speeches in which he said that the Hungarians in Vojvodina should be thrown out. Mr. Seselj says that this is stated in the report. Mr. Seselj says that he never said anything in this respect. In assuming that this is indeed in the report, that the report indeed says that the accused said that -- and he claims this is not true, because he says he never said that. If he's right, could this have any influence on your conclusions, to a slight or larger extent? Because if you drew conclusions from a report which is not absolutely true, would this not -- would this not have some consequences in your report? I believe now it's clear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not really. I didn't content analyse the Mazowiecki report on the mass media or the abuse of the -- of the mass media. I only content analysed Dr. Seselj's statements and speeches and TV appearances. So I never used Mazowiecki's report in my conclusions about Dr. Seselj. I only used Dr. Seselj's speech and -- and discourse in my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, you confirmed that there was an attack in Vojvodina on the Croat civilian population; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the Mazowiecki report or various Mazowiecki reports go into quite a lot of detail about very specific incidents that happened in particular places to particular people at certain dates, yes. There's a good -- there's a lot of documentation on that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were there attacks or an attack on the Croat civilian population? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they're described in those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where was the Croat civilian population in Vojvodina attacked? Please.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are mentions -- by the way, it was not just the Croat population. Some of them were Roma. Some of them were other minorities. And as I told you, if I had known that I would be specifically examined on something for which I am not here called to be an expert witness, I could have compiled page numbers from the Mazowiecki report to answer your question specifically. If -- if it's of real interest to you, I'm sure the research sections up on the second floor has all these reports and can give you all the detail that you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you now forget all about Mazowiecki and leave him completely aside. I'm asking you when, where, and how did attacks or an attack occur on the Croatian civilian population in Vojvodina? Because I claim there were no attacks on the Croat civilian population. You claim that there were. So tell me, what did they look like? Where did they happen? How long did they last? I'm interested. You made that claim here, and now you have to prove the veracity of your words.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I told you, the -- if -- if you really want to know -- and what I have said is based on these reports that we've been discussing, and this was not -- what happened in the Vojvodina in these years and the particular ethnic cleansing techniques and attacks was not part of what I was asked to provide expert advice to the -- to the Court, but I've read all those reports. And if you want to know the specifics that you asked me about, it's a matter of -- of really just an hour to get those reports, open the pages, and I could read you all the different places, occasions, targets of the ethnic cleansing that occurred in the Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may interject. The report in question is on the Prosecution's exhibit list at 65 ter number 1695. And if Mr. Seselj wants to question this witness further on the contents of the report or statements therein, I would request that he be given an opportunity to look at the document and familiarise himself with it. In the alternative, perhaps Mr. Seselj can move on, because it's not related to his expert report; the questioning is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the witness cannot answer this question. I see that he said there had been attacks. You put the question. He's not able to answer. So the Trial Chamber will draw its own conclusions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness was unable to answer when, how, and where this attack on civilian Croat population happened, so he cannot claim it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, let's on -- move on, Mr. Oberschall, to your main report. You, of course, claim - and that will be the subject of our discussion now - that I use untruths in my propaganda activities. You noted that propaganda means spreading certain information, regardless of whether it's true or not. And now you claim that I used untruths. So let us analyse a few of those claims you made. In your evidence about my theses and theories about the victimisation of Serbs, you say I often quote Serb victims and information about Serb victims in the Second World War; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reference to your untruths and misinformation and misuse of history is much more specific than that. For instance, I cite the best figures available on the -- the victims and the Serb -- the Serb deaths in the - I always have trouble pronouncing this - Jasenovac camp. So I specifically contrast the figures that you and some other people who are nationalists use with the figures that have been established by the association of victims from -- of this camp, and that's where I say that you have misinformed and are using the -- the wrong figures, inflated figures. My statements about you're misuse and misinformation, misuse of facts are always very specific. It doesn't deal with broad statements about victimisation of -- of Serbs or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Oberschall, that I state official figures, official figures of the Yugoslav state, that in total there was 1.700.000 victims in the Second World War in Yugoslavia; whereas, between 6 and 7 hundred thousand were killed in the Jasenovac camp. Do you know that this is official data?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you call official data, there's lots of official data. There's lots of unofficial data. There's lots of hypothetical data. There's a lot of fictional data. And what I am referring to is actual data based on research, whether it's official, unofficial, made up, hypothetical, or -- or what have you. You know, we're in -- we're in social science; we're not in this kind of history-writing to promote the cause of one group or another group. And I'm -- I sort of stay away from that and I contrast those figures with the best figures that are available on factual investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So to you, Mr. Oberschall, the most reliable is the figure found in the text of Srdjan Bogosavljevic. That's footnote 68 in your report. And that's the only footnote related to these figures. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I have to check this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Check. Check.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The material I am referring to is in my expert report on page 17, and specifically the figure that I refer to is in footnote 4 -- I mean, it refers -- footnote 4 gives a source. And what it says is that: "On the 60th anniversary of the death camp's liberation" - and we're talking about the Jasenovac - "the leaders of the Jasenovac death camp victims association stated that the Jasenovac museum had a list of 59.188 victims, and although the real number may never be known precisely, his association estimates them between 80 and 100 thousand, including Serb, Roma, Jewish, Croat, and other groups" were in that -- in that death count. So that's the figure that I think is the most reliable, because it is really the families of the victims that came forward and provided the information, and not some political party advocacy group, representatives of governments who had an interest in -- in inflating or deflating the figures. Generally the Serb sources inflated the figures; the Croat official and unofficial sources deflated the figures. And I use one where I thought that there was an interest on the part of a certain group to produce an accurate figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, do you know that this association of victims operates under the auspices of the Croatian government and that the Croatian government finances its activity through its own budget?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know about who sponsors, who finances this association. All I know is it's an association of the victims. And the victims include all the victims. It includes the Serb victims, the Croat victims, the Roma victims, the Jews, the -- the -- the other groups. It's -- it's not just one group that is made a membership in this association.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, do you know a single Roma who was in Jasenovac and left Jasenovac alive? Do you know of any such thing?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know personally any of the people --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- who died there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm already panic-stricken on account of time. Please give me answers that are as brief as possible. Do you know of a single Serb leaving Jasenovac alive?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Towards the end of the war there were some, but only 10 or 20. Mr. Oberschall, do you know who the only people who could survive Jasenovac were?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't see what this has to do with the number killed. You're talking now about the number who survived and whether I know the number survived. We're talking about the number who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'll explain that to you straight away. The association of victims is the association of survivors of Jasenovac, people who left Jasenovac alive; right? Only Croats could get out of Jasenovac alive and a few rich Jews. You could count them on the fingers of one hand. We have testimony, we have an enormous three-volume book written by Antun Miletic, a Croat, a colonel, about the camp of Jasenovac. He established that the Ustasha Croat authorities kept records only of camp inmates who were Croats and a few rich Jews. Serbs, masses of Jews, and all the Roma were just brought into Jasenovac and liquidated without keeping any record of that. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what you're saying is not true, because the -- the association does not include only the people who physically survived, but it includes the families of those who died. So what -- what you've been telling the -- the Court here in your testimony, it to me doesn't-- I mean, it doesn't really make any sense. Obviously an association of victims cannot be an association of the people who were killed. I mean, that's obvious. So it must be the survivors and the families of the survivors. It's not just the survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, there is a huge amount of literature about the Jasenovac camp. You did not consult it at all. You are basing your conclusions only on the report of a formally non-governmental Croatian organisation that is yet financed from the Croatian budget. Let us go back to footnote 68 that you're trying to evade. You mention Srdjan Bogosavljevic as the author of some article in a German publication from 1998. It is a five-page-long article. I don't know the German language. I see that it's something about genocide, but I cannot really quite understand that. You mentioned Srdjan Bogosavljevic as a reliable source in order to diminish the overall official figures of the victims of the Second World War in Yugoslavia. It is footnote 68. Do not evade this.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have any footnote 68. The pages that I have have all footnotes for every page going from 1 to about 6 or 7 and -- I -- I don't have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I've noted the problem, of course. In the expert report, footnotes are numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 per page. So each page it starts again, you know, at 1, 2, 3. So there can't be a footnote 68. So could you please tell us, what is this footnote 68?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think I see it. I think I -- I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've found it. So I don't have to look for it. Fine. You found Srdjan Bogosavljevic's footnote. In order to find my way more easily, I counted the footnotes, Judge, and this is the sixty-eighth footnote?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can protect the record here. We're at the English report, page 17, which is on the e-court screen presently, and we have the matching page in translation also by the court officer. It has been presented as well. And it appears that Mr. Seselj has renumbered the footnotes for his own use, rather than the translation which is consistent with the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Seselj, it seems that you have renumbered yourself all the footnotes, because we have the footnotes here on the screen and we have no "68" here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is footnote number 1 on page 16. Judge --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Answer it.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'd like to go back to the Jasenovac figures. Dr. Seselj says I never looked and did any research on it, which is not true. When I was in Zagreb in 1998, I -- I went to the -- the demographic unit in the Croat statistical service that -- they have a special unit that deals with these casualties and killings in World War II and -- and afterwards, and they produced figures for me and explained how they got the figures. I decided that the methodology was inadequate and that they were using -- that they were inflating their figures, and I simply did not use them because they were not reliable. So -- so that's why I'm not using those figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. This is what the Trial Chamber is interested in: You believe that it was about 60.000 victims and Mr. Seselj, what is his figure? We need to know that. And then it will be on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, the official figures are between 600 and 700 thousand victims. These are official data of Yugoslavia, and these were the figures used at the Nuremberg trials as well. However, we're not talking about Jasenovac now. Mr. Oberschall keeps evading Srdjan Bogosavljevic all the time. We're talking about the total number of victims. The official figure is 1.700.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You say it is less than 1.700.000. You say that it is at least 896.000 and the maximum is 1.210.000 deaths. That is what you say on page 17. And then you quote Srdjan Bogosavljevic. Please don't keep running away from Srdjan Bogosavljevic. He is a reliable source for you, as far as the number of victims in the territory of the former Yugoslavia in the Second World War are concerned. Is that right? Footnote 1, page 16. Or if we look at all the footnotes, it is the sixty-eighth footnote. In order to find my way there more easily, I had to renumerate this, but it doesn't really matter. It doesn't change anything.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it's absolutely true. The particular book that you're referring to that was in German contains a number of analyses of the deaths during World War II, deaths due to the war in -- in Yugoslavia. And several demographers and experts compared figures. Dr. Bogosavljevic looked and compared all these figures, and he himself is a -- an expert on these -- on these matters, and he came up with the figures that I felt were -- that you could defend -- you know, given the uncertainties, he gave kind of a range of -- of casualties that one could defend from a social science point of view. And that's what I've actually indicated here on page 17, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, you said that Srdjan Bogosavljevic was an expert in this type of demographic research. What makes him an expert or professional? Where is there proof of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether you're an expert or whether you're just a charlatan and a political hack who produces figures really depends on the reputation you have among your professional peers, not just in your own country and -- but -- but internationally. And what you should do in case you think that Dr. Bogosavljevic is not an expert, why don't you put his name into Google and see how many references there are by other demographers and experts to his work. And that -- that to me confirms whether somebody is a serious expert on a topic or whether he's just somebody who's being used politically for a -- you know, for propaganda purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's be brief. According to what you say, regarding this expert mentioned in this report, the number of Serb victims during World War II would be around 500.000. 500.000. Now, according to Mr. Seselj, could we know how many Serbs fell during World War II. Since you're challenging this -- the figure of this expert, give us your own figure. What do you estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, Srdjan Bogosavljevic did not deal with this issue seriously at all. He is no scholar who enjoys a proper reputation in academic circles in Serbia. He is the owner of Strategic Marketing, a privately owned agency in Serbia, and he is involved in political forecasts as to who is going to win an election, et cetera. His prognosis really depends on who pays him, and he doesn't really do any kind of serious work. He never wrote anything serious about victims in the Second World War. He uses data compiled by three authors here. Only three authors seriously challenge the number of Serb victims in the Second World War. Bogoljub Kocevic, who established a book about that in London in the 1970s. And this was published by an emigre organisation. And it was later -- it was led by the later leader or vice-president of the democratic party, Dasimir Tosevic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to speak slower, note the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Franjo Tudjman was the third one,.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the second one the interpreters did not catch.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None of them are demographic experts. One is an engineer. The other one was an independent publisher. And Franjo Tudjman, as you know, was a type of historian. I am not challenging the fact that he did achieve something in this scholarly field, but he's not a demographer. So that is what I wish to say to Mr. Oberschall. Where is the forgery here? And now I want to hear his position on this. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you're saying that three other people wrote about this, but the debate is whether it's 500.000, 1 million, 1.5 million. What exactly is your conclusion? Do you think that the figures that you gave us are your own -- are -- are true? And what is that figure? Because we still don't know it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I was not involved in such research. I have official figures. But I did establish how these three authors falsified the results of the research, and that is what I want to present to Mr. Oberschall, and then I want to hear his view on this. They worked on the basis of a census in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia before the Second World War and a census in communist Yugoslavia after the Second World War. They drew the following conclusion: That the number of Serb victims was exaggerated. And that the number of Muslim and Croat victims was diminished. Then they presented new figures with less Serbian victims and more, a lot more, Croat and Muslim victims, invoking the census. This is where the deception was. In the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, the census was carried out only on the basis of religion, not -- not ethnicity, because the Kingdom of Yugoslavia pursued a unitary policy. They wanted to create a Yugoslav nation. The Communists kept censuses only on the basis of ethnicity. They did not even have an entry for religious affiliation. So before the Second World War, we have a lot more Muslims than after the Second World War, because after the Second World War, when ethnicities were registered, many Muslims stated that they were Serbs and quite a few stated that they were Croats. That is where the deception is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you understand this deception, Mr. Oberschall? In statistics, these things cannot be compared. You have to have the same categories for different types of research in order to draw proper conclusions. You know what statistical methods consist of.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be given an opportunity to answer the question that Mr. Seselj has put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he can do it. You've heard the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did study demography and demographic methods, and Dr. Seselj just said that that's not part of what -- what he studied, and it's -- it's pretty obvious to me that -- that he didn't, given the -- what he's saying about all this. Let me just say that on the basis of the papers by demographers that I looked at which are in this volume, my assessment was that the Bogosavljevic analysis of the various claims and figures, some of which were inflated, some of which were obviously diminished, depending on which political side one came from -- and he weighed all these considerations and the methodology, and I came to the conclusion that he in fact gave you a pretty good range, 460.000 to 590.000 on Serbs and Montenegrins, and Croats 190 to 270 thousand, that that was just about as good an estimate as could be done given what there is available by way of -- by way of factual evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Please continue, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm already panic-stricken that too much time was taken up only by one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the same page in the next paragraph, you wrote: When speaking to the author of this report, "a university student in Belgrade recalls a Serb writer asserting before a student club in 1990" -- and then quotation marks -- it doesn't matter what the student said. What was the name of the student who said this to you in Belgrade, Mr. Oberschall?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I have, of course, recorded in my field notes, but I don't see how that's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the footnote, in footnote 5, you say that this conversation took place on the 27th of May, 1998. That's your reference; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is the name of this Serb author who was asserting something before a student club in 1990? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I have it -- I have it recorded in my -- in my field notes, and I didn't think it was important to -- to give the name of this particular speaker that the student talked about. I could have used many other quotes, by the way, from these interviews that I did in -- in Belgrade at the time, but they're -- they're all pretty much the same type of information that was provided to me, and it had to do with the fact that there was pretty routine political discourse by Serb intellectuals and media about rape, atrocities, conspiracy stories, and I merely just quote for the sake of on the -- being on the record what one of these students told me. I could have had a lot of other quotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're giving me answers that are too extensive and there's no substance in them. Mr. Oberschall, how can a scholar, a scientist, in an expert report invoke by way of an argument the fact that one student - we don't know what student; you know in your secret papers. In the report, there's no trace of that - that one student said to him that he recalls that a Serb writer a few years ago asserted something before a student club? Is this really fitting for a serious scholar and scientist, Mr. Oberschall?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I mean, I wasn't asked to write a 300-page book about everything that's possible to write about mass media propaganda and -- and your statements and -- and the Serb media. I was -- I was asked to write a concise easily understandable summary with -- with a lot of detail, but not everything conceivable that could be put into such a -- you know, a much -- much larger volume. And that's what I did. I had to be selective on certain quotes, including the quotes that come from the content analysis. I could have each time listed your 47 threats every time we talk about -- that I -- that I analysed threats. But I only selected three or four. If somebody is interested in the full record, they can look through the -- the full documentation that I give in the appendix.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, let's go back to methodology of scientific research. Can science sustain a method where the author uses the following construction: A man told me that a while ago another man had told him. Is this a scientific approach?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- about -- what you're referring to is whether information can be used that is in books, that somebody who uses that information didn't actually have a personal experience, referring to the events that he cites in the books; whether he can quote other people in interviews; whether he can -- whether he can use information that somebody tells him happened to them at an earlier time. And yes, if -- if it's well-documented, all of that information can be used and, you know, has to be analysed and sifted carefully, but it can be used in scientific discourse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, you submitted your expert report in order to support the indictment. If that indictment is proven to be true, then I will spend my life in prison. And in this report, you say that a man told you that a while ago another man had said to him, and so on and so forth. And in response to my questions, you don't know the name of either men. And you came here knowing that I would submit you to relentless cross-examination. Now, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does -- what does what mean? I mean, what's -- what's the question here? It's -- it's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, time is precious for me. I'm not going to insist on this any longer. I see that you have no answer whatsoever. Let's move on, and during the remaining half hour let me try to put a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please don't let the Prosecutor use my time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's going to move on to something else. So why did you want to intervene?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Either Mr. Seselj can rephrase the question that the witness hasn't understood or he can withdraw it, but it is inappropriate for him to comment that the witness is not answering a question when in fact the witness has asked for clarification of a question he did not understand. So I object to improper cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Move on to something else, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you going to deduct this from my time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, on page 17, towards the bottom, you say that I was persistently warning the Serbs that there was the danger of pan-Islamism, and so on. Do you think that these threats were not real?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wrote is that a group of writers analysed the discourse on the radio and television of Belgrade and Serbia about the Bosnian war, and that's what they concluded. The theme was the Muslims are Jihad warriors, criminals, slaughterers, Islamic Ustashas, Mujahedin, terrorists, and extremists. So yes, that's -- that's in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, do you know that the communist regime in 1986 prohibited by court order my book "A hunt for heretics," where I warned against fundamentalist and pan-Islamist threats in 1986?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't -- I don't know about that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you, Mr. Oberschall, believe that in Bosnia and Herzegovina there exists a Muslim nation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a people that call themselves Bosniaks and many of them also call themselves Muslims, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, from what year are they called Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that happened sometime during the war. I don't know the exact date at which they ... By the way, that excludes -- that includes also some Serbs and Croats who decided to stay in the federation and -- and become citizens of basically the federation. So we're not only talking about Muslims. We're talking about a number of other groups. The majority are Muslims. At what day did the term "Bosniak" come into general use? I don't know. But sometime during the war to distinguish the Republika Srpska from the other groups who wanted to maintain a -- a unified Bosnia as a successor state in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, thus it's a nation that was proclaimed some 10 or 15 years ago. Before that, it didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you have -- you are always confusing what is official recognition and the actual consciousness and identity and self-definition of a -- of a people. I have pointed this out in my expert report on -- on several occasions, and I don't know what I can do to, you know, remove that confusion in your mind. I've referred to all the sources, starting in the history of modern nationalism, starting with the French historian Renan who gave this lecture at the Sorbonne about "What is a nation?" And I quote some other sources down to the contemporary view of nationalism and you always have rejected that kind of terminology that is accepted throughout the world. You talk about artificial nations. You talk about, you know, all kinds of euphemism where you deny the -- the self-definition and the accepted sense of -- of -- of being a people that -- that is a -- is a product of culture and history. You always belittle that. You deny that. You think some kind of an official statement that something exists and something doesn't exist really makes all the difference in this whole process. So my answer to you is there were people who called themselves Muslim, who identified themselves as Muslim in Bosnia since pretty much the Turkish -- the Turkish times, seventeenth century on. And whether the officials recognize it or didn't recognize it or whether it be -- were part of a peace treaty or an agreement doesn't really make any difference. What makes the difference is how they viewed themselves and how others viewed themselves. And they were recognized as a people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You refer to Renan and that's an absolute stronghold for you. Do you know who Schelling was? Do you know what Schelling's definition of a nation is?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the German philosopher?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He gave a definition of "nation."

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't quote to you what his definition of "nation" is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I will quote it. According to Schelling, "nation" is language. And now, Mr. Oberschall, to refute this thesis of yours and the suffering that you ascribe to me. Just imagine, France is a state with 60 million population, between 50 and 60 million, if I remember correctly. Now, imagine, in one part of France - let's say that it's the environs of Marseilles or the environs of Paris, any French city - 5 million French people decide to convert to Islam. And that's their right. We had this famous French philosopher, Roger Garaudy, who converted sometime in the 1970s to Islam. You heard about him, I hope. He was a philosopher of Marxist orientation, later converted to the Islam philosophy. Do you know who Roger Garaudy is? Imagine that his example was followed by 5 million French. Original French people, not immigrants. They say, we are now embracing Islam, and from this moment we are the -- an Islamic nation. Would that be sufficiently good reason for you to say that they are an Islamic nation, because that's the way they feel?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, you're making completely, you know, strange kind of statements and assumptions. If people in France or anywhere else convert to any kind of a religion, individually or in large groups, it makes absolutely no difference whatsoever to what their citizenship and whether or not they consider themselves a nation. They -- they consider themselves a religious -- having a same religious faith. It doesn't interfere with their citizenship or any other kind of sense that they are in this case Frenchmen. So I don't know -- you're just living in a different world from -- from the real world, as far as I'm concerned. I mean, you're -- you're troubling yourself with all kinds of hypothetical and strange questions that have no relevance to contemporary history.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You are unable to answer a perfectly logical question of mine. I'm not talking about citizenship. Of course, hypothetically French people who would convert to Islam would remain citizens of France. But if they do what Bosnian Muslims have done and say, We are no longer Serbs. We are now an Islamic nation. Would you then, based on the frame of their mind, say that they are indeed a Muslim nation within France? That's my question. It's perfectly logical.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the Muslims never said that -- that they were Serbs and all of a sudden that they became non-Serbs. They -- they said they were Muslims all along, ever since the -- ever since Turkish times. I don't know. It's very confusing. You know, your thinking about all this, it -- it kind of mixes all kind of things up. You can be a citizen, be a member of a religious community that's a minority of all the religious faiths in that community. You can speak a language which is in fact spoken by a minority of the people in that state, and you can still consider yourself a -- not just a citizen but, as I am considering myself an American, or a Frenchman would consider himself a Frenchman. We have multiple identities. Not all those identities most of the time make a claim to having to have some kind of a sovereign state representing them in a particular territory. There's a sort of -- this is basic social psychology and basic history. And -- and what can I say? I mean, I lecture on this to my students, and it's a shame that you did not take the courses that -- that I taught on this topic, because your thinking wouldn't be muddled and confused about all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the public and the Trial Chamber will be able to judge who is muddled and confused. I can only laugh at what you just said. It's perfectly obvious who's muddled and confused here. Mr. Oberschall, what happened to us Serbs over several centuries, a part of it under -- a part of the people under the Turkish occupation convert to Islam and identify with the occupier, and the other part converts to Catholicism and gradually loses Serbian national awareness. I'm now speaking on the basis of historical facts. We are Serbs Orthodox, they are Catholic Serbs, and the third part are Muslim Serbs, regardless of what they feel like, because this quarrel was imposed on us in a religious war, but I keep saying that we are still one nation.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you didn't ask me a question. You just made a declaration. Other people have different views about this, and that's your view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, you are putting it to me in your report that I deny the existence of the Macedonian nation. That's also in the report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, then, why then don't the United Nations recognize the Macedonian nation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's -- that's -- that's really true. The question has nothing to do with the Macedonian people. It has to do with the state of Macedonia. And it -- it has to do with the objection of the Greek government to the use of the term "Macedonia," which also describes part of Northern -- Northern Greece. So we have a dispute here not about a nation or a people or what they're called. We have a dispute about the -- the title or the -- the official UN and diplomatic way of describing a particular state. There's no challenge to the territory of that state or the boundaries of that state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There is no dispute about the territory and the boundaries, because the Macedonian population is mostly Slav. However, Greece does dispute the name of the state and the name of the nation and the name of the language; isn't that correct? And they say, This state cannot be called Macedonia. That nation cannot be called Macedonian. And that language cannot be called Macedonian. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be correct, but the Greeks say -- I don't know. I haven't studied what the Greek government maintains or who among the Greeks maintains that..

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Why then did not the European Union recognize the name of the State of Macedonia and the name of the Macedonian people and the name of the Macedonian language? Why didn't the European Union do that? Because Macedonia claims to become a member of the European Union one day but under its current name, the former Yugoslavia Republic of Macedonia; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you -- you've asked a lot of things at -- at the -- at the same time, so I -- I don't know what precisely do you want me to say or -- or answer. I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't expect anything. I have no more time. I'm moving on to the next question. Mr. Oberschall, more than once yesterday you said - and that's also in your report - that I advocate amputation of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was I the first to use that wording, "amputation of Croatia"?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who was the first?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't do a -- a history of -- of the various terms and phrases that you used. Some of it you shared with other people; some of it come from people who preceded you. I'm -- I wasn't doing that kind of linguistic research.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, I'll tell you. The first to use that wording was the Yugoslavia King Aleksandar Karadjordjevic in 1928. And since then it has circulated in our historical and political discourse. Many other politicians picked it up in their own studies and explained what this idea of amputation means. Unfortunately, it wasn't performed in good time. But that's another issue. Mr. Oberschall, you spoke here about the liberal democratic discourse within the European Union.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you derived the difference between that discourse and the Serbian political discourse. Have you heard of Jean Cot? He is a French general, former UNPROFOR commander in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it wasn't true that I compared the -- the European Union, what I called the civic nationalist discourse, with the Serb discourse. I -- I compared it to the nationalist -- xenophobic nationalist discourse, and that includes a lot more people, intellectuals, statesmen, than just Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I asked you if you had heard of Jean Cot. I told you who he was. In a statement for "Defense Nationale" newspaper, he stated in June 1997: "As far as Serbs are concerned, nowadays it's a sick people, poisoned a long time ago. They have been -- become a victim of a collective paranoia." Is this liberal democratic discourse?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually it's generalisation and stereotype and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I'd like the witness to be allowed to complete his answer. This is improper cross-examination to interrupt the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was a bit missing. You were talking about stereotypes. Did you want to add anything? Because in the transcript, you see, you wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. What I -- what I wanted to add is that even though it is true that the xenophobic nationalist discourse prevailed at this time in Serbia, it doesn't mean that all Serb intellectuals -- and in fact, many outstanding Serb writers and politicians actually used and thought, in terms of what I call the civic nationalist discourse -- they happened to be on the losing side politically. I would never characterise all Serbs as having a uniform ideology or a point of view about anything like nationalism and -- and -- and many other things. In fact, I talked to -- to some of them, and they in fact have political parties they contest elections. So I just want to make -- put that into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall seems to be a machine for wasting my precious time. I had a specific question, and I want only specific answers. I don't want his opinion on various subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, listen to me carefully. The former President of France, Jacques Chirac, at a time when he was President of France, at a summit of heads of states of the European Union, in June 1995 in Paris, interrupted the speech of the Greek Prime Minister, Andreas Papandreou, who said that a civil war was going on in Bosnia with many features of a religious war. And here Jacques Chirac says: "Allow me to interrupt you, Prime Minister. Serbs are a people without law and without religion. It's a nation of highway robbers and terrorists." It was broadcast on EuroNews in June 1995. My associate then, Dejan Mirovic, quoted that in my notification of special defence that I submitted to the Prosecution two years ago, and it's otherwise published in a book by Zoran Petrovic "Erase the Serbian virus," 2002. Would this statement by Jacques Chirac be part of the liberal democratic discourse? Would it fall within those boundaries?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I very much doubt that President Chirac ever said what is attributed to him. If -- if you actually cited a French newspaper or journalist rather than this sort of roundabout citations and attributions, you know, then I would react and assess what President Chirac said. I would feel confident that he in fact said it. What you quote here and the sources that you describe, and so on, to me is just not reliable. There's a lot of fact and fiction and propaganda that -- that goes on in -- in this kind of, you know, attempt to justify yourself and attack other people. And if you give me a statement that I feel confident that derives from President Chirac on the Serbs in this -- in this war, then I will react to it. But I -- I don't react to this kind of hearsay stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, the day before yesterday you mentioned the president of Venezuela, Mr. Hugo Chavez. And you quoted him as an example. You said that he was an example of a political leader who is closer to my discourse. That's what you said the day before yesterday here in the courtroom. Do you remember that? It's on the record. I noted your statement.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess if it's on the record -- if it's on the record, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Oberschall. I believe Hugo Chavez to be one of the leaders of freedom-loving humanity, because he is opposed to American leadership, globalism, or whatever it's called. Hugo Chavez took part a few days ago at the summit of --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I object to a speech about Mr. Seselj's views of Hugo Chavez. This is improper cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your views on Mr. Chavez are not to be taken into account, unless based on a question, you put a question to the witness, and he can answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do have a question, but the Prosecutor didn't allow me to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Here is the question: A few days ago there was a summit of Hispano-American states. Did you see it on TV? It was on CNN, on BBC, on various French televisions and Dutch televisions that I'm able to see here. They showed it all. Have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I mean, I follow the news, so -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: An incident occurred when the Spanish king, Juan Carlos, jumped up and started insulting Hugo Chavez. All the televisions in the world broadcast that. Have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, do you believe the Spanish king, Juan Carlos, to be someone who propounds liberal democratic discourse?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say why the Spanish king said what he did, is because Hugo Chavez insulted Spain, Spanish history, and -- and used a totally undiplomatic, inappropriate language in that kind of an international meeting of -- of -- of heads of state. And that's why he walked out. That's why the King Juan Carlos walked out. And I think he was right that he should walk out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Oberschall. Hugo Chavez was talking about historical facts. Spaniards were very brutal in colonizing Latin America, looting and killing everything before them, setting the land on fire. It's a historical fact, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, do you really want to talk about the history of Spain in the Americas for the remaining -- for the remaining time that you have? I mean, is this a -- is this a course, a seminar on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he's asking a question. You can say "I know," "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I know all that history he's referring to. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you say you know. Fine. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the president of Venezuela, Hugo Chavez, elected at democratic elections by the will of his people?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right. Now, was the Spanish king, Juan Carlos, elected democratically by the will of his people?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Spanish king does not get elected by a popular vote, because he's recognized in the constitution of the country, but it's not an elected office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Oberschall. Do you know who put the Spanish king, Juan Carlos, on the restored Spanish throne?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know really quite how that happened. It -- it had to do in the last years of the Franco regime. There was a constitutional settlement. I'm not prepared to talk about the details of the Spanish history in that kind detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, go to the actual question, Mr. Seselj, because your time is just about up. Please put your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my time has run out, I'll ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Spanish king, Juan Carlos, was put on that throne. The fascist dictator, Francisco Franco, that was his own personal decision. On one hand, we have Hugo Chavez, who was elected democratically by the Venezuelan people, by democratic elections. On the other hand, we have the Spanish king, Juan Carlos, who was placed on the throne by a fascist dictator. Now, Juan Carlos you believe to be a proponent of liberal democratic discourse and you believe Hugo Chavez to be a proponent of the discourse that is opposed to liberal democratic discourse which is closer to mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be a mistake in the transcript, because I see the Omarska camp suddenly has nothing to do with it. The question has been put to you, please answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to point out that just about three weeks ago in a referendum in Venezuela, Hugo Chavez wanted to confirm, assuming dictatorial powers, and he lost that referendum by, I think, about 52:4 against and 48 in favour. So you keep talking about Hugo Chavez as representing the -- the Venezuelan people and being an elected politician. But the majority of his countrymen are actually him against him at this present time. And they made it very clear that they are against him. Now, you're asking me questions about comparing a constitutional monarch and his legitimacy to speak for his -- for his people with a elected head of state, and I -- I really don't understand what all this has to do with a -- with a topic that we're considering here. I must say I've forgotten now exactly where we are in this all, in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, this question on comparing the King of Spain with Mr. Chavez, what was purpose of it? Because we have difficulty in following you. What was the purpose of your question as part of your cross-examination, in relation to the expert report? What did you want to highlight? Which truth did you want to highlight?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am showing how untenable this construction is that Mr. Oberschall refers to in his expertise, that on the one hand, there is liberal democratic discourse, and, on the other hand, this nationalist discourse, which is not liberal and democratic at the same time. Hugo Chavez wanted to have his constitutional authority extended. He held a referendum and by a slim majority the people said, We won't allow this. And Hugo Chavez immediately admitted that. The people do not want to have my authority extended. That's part of the democratic process. He proved to be a democrat there; whereas, the King of Spain, the King of Spain never called a referendum to check what the will of the people was in relation to the will of Franco the dictator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, you wanted the floor?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The volume of Mr. Seselj's voice in the courtroom is preventing me from hearing him in translation. And I would like to be able to follow what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely right. Mr. Seselj, you've explained yourself. You explained why you wanted to ask this question. But your time is up. You've used up the time that the Trial Chamber had allotted you. Will Mrs. Dahl have any redirect? No? Fine. Then, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have time to put all my questions, but I'm not complaining. I would just like, if possible, for you to admit into evidence two documents that I prepared. I don't know whether Mr. Oberschall received this in English, this proclamation to the Serbs of the Muslim faith that I signed in 1990, and it was published in the first volume of Velika Srbija. And also part of the editorial of this first volume of Velika Srbija. Has this been submitted to you, Mr. Oberschall? The service was supposed to submit that to you. They're giving it to you only now? I had hoped that you would be provided with this earlier on. Another thing, Mr. President: You did not accept my official notification with regard to the second addendum related to the expert report of Witness Oberschall, and I submitted that on the 26th of November. I went beyond the deadline. However, the Trial Chamber can extend every one of the deadlines envisaged in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. So I ask you, then, to admit this into evidence, and the translation can be deducted from that quota of 10.000 pages that you've allowed me; so that can be part of that quota. I have submitted this early enough for Mr. Oberschall and the Prosecution to familiarise themselves with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You're asking for the -- this to be tendered, and the Prosecution will answer. You're asking to tender a document that was disclosed to the Trial Chamber and to the Prosecution just a few minutes ago. That's one document. And the second document is the rejoinder -- is the addendum that the Trial Chamber had not admitted because the deadline had not been complied with. What is the position of Prosecution regarding these two requests?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I think procedurally that would be a Defence exhibit marked for identification, but I have no objection if Mr. Seselj wants to make sure we proceed efficiently, if he wants exhibits admitted in the Prosecution's case in chief. We'll take them and -- and move forward. I do, however, in the face of this, have one brief question on redirect perhaps I can ask Dr. Oberschall after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we have no break.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please ask your question right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Dr. Oberschall, did you have an opportunity to look at Mr. Seselj's book entitled "The ideology of Serbian nationalism"? Specifically, the -- the chapter headings in his book.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- actually, I have them with me here, the chapter headings.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Okay. Would you take a moment to look at the subchapter headings for Mr. Seselj's views on Croats in a historical perspective.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. First of all, yesterday Mr. Oberschall said that he never had my book "The ideology of Serb nationalism" in my hands, and that exhausted my question. Secondly, in the re-examination the Prosecutor only has the right to deal with questions that had already been raised during the examination-in-chief or the cross-examination. She does not have the right to start new topics now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, it seems that regarding this book, you said that you did not read it. And now you're saying that you know the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can -- if I can clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've only seen the Table of Contents. I didn't -- I didn't read the book. Just the Table of Contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you know the Table of Contents. Secondly, regarding the objection on the additional question, what is the basis of this additional question? Does it have anything to do with the question asked by Mr. Seselj during the cross?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, it did, Your Honour. We presented the texts in electronic format that were searchable. We didn't send the -- the expert the physical books that he -- Mr. Seselj was holding up. And I wanted to cover the characterisation of Croats by Mr. Seselj in his book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is the following: What question did Mr. Seselj ask to the witness which is the basis for this new question that you are asking?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The question concerned the accuracy of Mr. Seselj's characterisations of Croats in history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So ask your question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, Judge, an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, when was it that I discussed that yesterday and the day before yesterday? There was no mention of that. If you remember, my first question this morning addressed to Mr. Oberschall was whether yesterday afternoon or last night or this morning he discussed the subject of his testimony with anyone. He said he did not. All of a sudden he appears with the contents of my book. Obviously he had contact with someone regarding this. Please don't allow that. Ms. Dahl will have an opportunity to call other witnesses with regard to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Seselj. This is not the question. This is not the problem. During the cross-examination, you did talk about Croats, Croat victims, and so on. You did address this topic. It's a very broad topic. And the Prosecution can ask for an additional information about this, and this is what Mrs. Dahl wants to do. So let's ask -- let's wait for the question. You are asking for the floor and you don't even know what the question. Mrs. Dahl, please ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Could you please read the characterisations of Mr. Seselj in his subchapters and then comment in the coding analysis that you did on what categories that description of Croats would fall into.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here -- here are the subchapters' titles: "Europe horrified by the Croat's bloodthirstiness," "Incredible criminal effluence of the Croatian mindset creates as a paradigm of cruelty," "Croatian barbarity in folk songs," "Croatian massacre -- massacres in Ham [phoen]," "Croatian history abounds with savagery, robbery and murder as a primordial feature of the Croatian national character," "Croats as a blind tool of the Vatican," "The bestial urges of the Croatian ethnic being." I -- I didn't read every one of them, but they pretty much are the same. First of all, they are -- this is pretty extreme talk. It's very negative stereotypes. Some of it actually falls into the category that I didn't use when I read the other texts, which is "Dehumanisation." I mean, the bestial urges of the Croatian ethnic being is like comparing a human being to an inferior, almost like a -- a prehuman primate or other kind of animal. So -- and, of course, all of it would be generalisations, because, you know, we're talking about all the Croats. And that's -- that's how I would have coded it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, in traditional propaganda techniques, what would someone use these kinds of dehumanisations or generalisations to achieve?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it would -- it would create fear of these bestial beings. Secondly, it would create animosity against them, mistrust, inability to -- to deal with them on a civilised cooperative level. I mean, with savages, and so on. So that would be -- that would be the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The uses of these kind of propaganda to create these kind of sentiments and inimical relationships, hostile relationships, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Oberschall. Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague has a question. He read the titles of the chapters in your book and he did answer as to the propaganda technique employed. What more do you want?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Judge, I ask you not to allow an analysis on the basis of -- an analysis of a text on the basis of contents at the very end of that book. This has to do with testimony of historical eyewitnesses and prominent European historians, military leaders, and even the great German poet, Schiller, who described Croats that way in his own ballad. And the Croats in the Cilician wars, killed the entire population of Magdeburg in Germany, near Dresden. And a content analysis cannot be carried out on the basis of the contents of a book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Given the time, perhaps we should take the break now and I'll put my questions after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have any time left? Because it would be best to finish off. Mr. Registrar, how much time do we have left regarding the tape? Why have a 20-minute break and come back just for a few minutes? I believe we have five or ten minutes left on the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Oberschall, I have a few questions relating to something which I don't think has been brought up by any of the parties; namely, the methods used in your expert report. And the first question I wanted to put to you relates to what you have indicated in page 1 of your report, because I wanted to know what was the question that was put to you by the Prosecution in order for you to work on this report. And I see that on the top of the page there is a question that reads: "How mass media propaganda impacts on ordinary people's acceptance and participation in collective violence" and "How Seselj's nationalist propaganda promoted and justified coercion and violence by Serbs against non-Serbs." And my question is: Was that the question that was put to you by the Prosecution? Was this your task?
