utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the -- as I recall what I was asked to do is to content analyse the political discourse of Dr. Seselj on Serb/non-Serb political relations during the time that was indicated, 1991 to 1994. Of course, that was a nationalist discourse and -- and I was asked to provide sort of an expert opinion of that discourse, and I immediately said for that we have to do a content analysis, because this is the only way that you can, instead of searching and picking particular statements, get a -- a good record and do a uniform analysis. And, you know, that's what's sort of currently done in -- in political discourse analysis, is based on content analysis, rather than just a selection. So they said yes: Can you do that? And I said yes, I can do it and I will do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'll get to that in just a minute. My question is: Who then formulated this passage that I just read it out?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because that seems to be a working thesis.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. Because I didn't think that one could meaningfully as a social scientist just produce a set of conclusions based on the sort of narrow propaganda analysis of counts, you know, how many threats, how many victimisation statements without putting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, did this working hypothetical question or thesis, did that in fact guide you through your study? Was that the --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What thesis are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The question that I have read out to you, and I'll -- which is on the top of page 1, the issue: How mass media -- and I'll read it again, if you didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. My question is: These two questions that are included to here, did they form the working thesis for you when you were doing your study?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Propaganda analysis, whether it's content analysis or otherwise, deals with three basic questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, please --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The messenger, the message, and the impact that it has. And the impact it that has is a very important part of propaganda analysis. And as much as possible, I went into the impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You see, we are at the beginning of the trial here.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And you have presented a report. And for the Chamber to understand fully the value and the use of your report, I have to be sure about what your study purported to show. And so this is why my question relates to the opening thesis that you -- I want to deal with the question of how media propaganda impacts on ordinary people -- on ordinary people's acceptance and participation in collective violence and how Seselj's nationalist propaganda promoted and justified coercion. So that's why -- that's -- my question is to ascertain whether this was in fact what you wanted to prove, to --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- talk to these topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is good to know. Because then, if you move on to part -- to page 2, you describe the methodology of your content analysis. And in the big paragraph, which is just below the middle of the page --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- you say that "Oberschall" -- this is yourself, I suppose -- "identified the following themes on which information was necessary to fully characterise Seselj's views and positions." And then you list -- you line out all the keywords that you used subsequently in your analysis of each piece of material that you got from the Prosecution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Now, my question is: How did you arrive at these keywords?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explained that here, and it's looking at the literature on nationalism -- that is the best sources I could find on nationalism, like people like Anthony Smith, who is the, you know, the Oxford professor who keeps writing about nationalism, and other authors. And in their books on nationalist discourse, they list a number of topics, such as being presented as a victim, trying to make a connection between being a chosen or a special people who has sometimes in a religious sense of being a chosen people by God or by history or by destiny. So I looked very carefully at what their major themes were, and I then produced the -- the glorification, the negative stereotypes, all of that is in this literature, specifically in Anthony Smith's book that I referred to. So I compiled this list of what I was going to look for, which is my coding categories from the literature on nationalism. There's another five -- or six coding items which comes from the literature on the techniques of propaganda. The generalisation, stereotyping, threat messages, victimisation, and so on. These -- it doesn't matter whether you -- you look at contemporary or nineteenth century documents or -- or speeches or -- or -- or whatever, of whatever people. There are techniques of propaganda which are pretty much the same. So I coded both for the nationalist themes from the nationalism literature and the techniques of propaganda from the propaganda literature, and the discourse is a combination of techniques and the substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I -- I realize that you have probably struck most of the issues which would be relevant to assess in the examination that you have carried out, but you see, for the Chamber it's important to know whether each of these 11 topics that you have listed out in your --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- methodology --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- were things that you were -- were issues that you had selected from literature or whether some of these issues were issues that you had figured out yourself as being relevant for this analysis.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were -- of course, when I -- when I said "threats," I had to specify it has threats involving Serbs or against Serbs. So I added that. But in the literature on nationalism deals with the relationship between many different kinds of people and religious groups, and so sometimes you would have French and German and Russians in there specifically, but I was only dealing with Serbs and non-Serbs, so I specified within this nationalist discourse that -- that -- that the threats and the victimisation referred to Serbs and to non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I -- I think that maybe I'm not expressing myself clearly in my question, so I'll try again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The issue is whether each of these 11 topics that you have chosen for your analysis have been derived from -- from scientific literature that you have gone through or whether you developed them yourself for the purpose of this analysis.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- I derived them from the -- what -- the scientific literature; however, I left out some topics which did not really apply and don't ever appear in Dr. Seselj's discourse; that is, in the -- in the -- the nationalist literature, there's often parallels made between nation and religion and sort of a quasi-religious discourse about being a chosen people and favoured by God and that kind of -- that kind of nationalist religious terminology. If I were to analyse al-Qaeda or -- or Osama bin Laden's discourse, I would have to include here things that have to do with religion, but in the -- in the kind of secular nationalist discourse that Dr. Seselj conducted, this never appears, so I just left it out, even though it was in the literature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you selected these 11 topics as being the most relevant and thereby --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- deciding to leave out some that you thought were not relevant. The -- the reason I'm asking, of course, is that -- that in those topics, I would have thought that references to what might be characterised as the accused's paradigms or his views of how Serbs should be regarded in contemporary history would be a relevant parameter to include also.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did that in my report when I -- of course, I coded for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It doesn't figure here as -- as one of the topics that you used for analysis.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I had a general code called "nations and nationalities"; that is to say, Dr. Seselj's discourse on nations and nationalities. He actually gave us a couple of examples today. And by then going into the detailed views that he put forward in these texts about the Serbs being a true nation and the other peoples in Yugoslavia being artificial nations and what are nations and what are people and what are -- you know, Macedonians are not nations, Montenegrins are Serbs but don't know it, and that kind of thing, is what I then covered in other sections of my report, especially the section on "Seselj's discourse -- nationalist discourse." And that's when I go into the specific examination of the texts that I coded under "nations and nationals -- nationalism."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. If you then move to the next category, which you have called "persuasion."

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where -- what page are we on now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: On any of the pages that -- that -- on the record numbers. You can pick any record number and you will see underneath --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- you have these 11 topics and then you have seven means of persuasion.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And there you list out stereotyping, generalisation, falsehood, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would have thought that the context in which each of his statements were made would have an impact on your assessment of the persuasiveness. Would it not make a difference whether these -- whether the speech that the accused was giving was given, say, in a radio programme or in a public newspaper or in a crowd at a demonstration, or whatever? Or does that not make any difference?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I'm coding for here is not persuasion in the sense of impact. I'm coding for technique of persuasion. From the context of what I am coding, which is a text, I have no information about how the radio or the TV audience or people who read the newspaper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, we'll have to have a break, a ten-minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may just finish. I have a whole section in my expert report on the impact and how I measured impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen, we're going to have a break, unfortunately, for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have resumed the hearing. Judge Harhoff is going to proceed with his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Oberschall, what you were telling me before the break was that the seven headings under the "persuasion" group is not actually physical persuasion but, rather, techniques of persuasion.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If we return to the original working thesis, as you had put it out on page 1, I would revert to the second question that you put up for yourself; namely, "how Seselj's nationalist propaganda promoted and justified coercion and violence by the Serbs against non-Serbs." This last part of your working thesis would suggest that you had actually conducted studies into the effects of Dr. Seselj's speeches and things. Did you do so?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain what I -- what I did. When it comes to the impact of propaganda discourse, the findings that I referred to about threat messages creating fear and being powerful in terms of action derive from social psychological experiments, a lot of them done at Yale University, over a period of time in which you always have a control group, you have an experimental group that gets the messages and a control group that receives other messages, and then a comparison is made on sort of before and after what their thinking is, what their beliefs are, what their sentiments are. Now, it's not possible to do this kind of experimental work in a natural historical setting. So there's sort of other ways, which are not as -- as good, but still there are other ways of trying to measure propaganda impacts. The most important media is television. Now, one -- one problem with measuring the impacts of television is it's very hard to find in the contemporary age a part of the population that is not exposing itself to television, because, you know, viewers are all over the place and the majority of the people look at television, not just -- you know, in every country. So what I tried to do is to find a measure of what is an impact, and that is a vote, a vote in elections. So I tried to find -- and I refer to two situations in which Dr. Seselj had access to the -- to the -- to the media of communication before an election, and then look at an election shortly afterwards when for -- because of his rivalry with the -- with the Milosevic regime he actually was deprived of such access, or even more, he was negatively depicted in the -- in the media of communication, in -- in television. And I found two such examples. And then I compared the votes that he got when he held his discourse on the -- the Serb media compared to the votes that he got when he didn't have that opportunity, or a much more limited opportunity, and looked at the number of votes that he got. In -- in one case, it was two elections that were about a few months apart. In another case, actually only three weeks apart, because it was a run-off, you know, as you -- you know from ... Okay. So by looking at those figures and the election outcomes, as provided by Goati, I estimated that lack of access and -- or negative depicting of him in the media cost him or his party something like between 20 and 40 per cent of the votes that he would count on compared to when he had access to TV. So to me that's a pretty good measure of impact. I don't know what else and how else to measure the impact, but it's a political impact and Dr. Seselj was pretty much not changing his position, his policies, his views. He had a fairly constant political discourse at this time, so that's the measure of impact that I came up with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So in your study, you were able to show that the accused's speeches had an impact on peoples exercising their democratic rights.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That would seem to me to be quite different from what you have set out in your working thesis; namely, that you wanted to show how the nationalist -- nationalist propaganda promoted and justified coercion and violence by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's two very different things that --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his discourse, as I've done and examined in a content analysis, is a pretty aggressive nationalist discourse justifying Greater Serbia and an expansionist policy, including armed conflict against -- against the neighbouring states. So that's what he -- that's what they were reacting to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was his discourse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One follow-up question. If I understand you properly, in fact when there is an election, the media are the ones that are going to cause the results. Depending on the access or lack of access by the candidates, the results will be influenced by the media or a consequence of the media. Is that the conclusion one is to draw?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- not really. That is to say, when he does not have the media, that is to say, he doesn't have television and probably also radio, of course he still has the -- the party newspaper, the election rallies, the speeches he makes at -- at the Assembly, and so on. And that produces, in my estimate which I give in this report, something like 600.000 votes that this party and he can count on. But when he does have the extra access to television where his message is not only directed at the readers of the -- of the Radical newspaper and an audience that pays -- goes to his rallies, and supporters that he already has, so to speak, then he can increase his votes from about 600 -- 5, 6 hundred thousand, to about a million.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you say. However, in your theory, what do you make of the free decision, the free power to decide of a citizen, of the one who listens to a speech, who watches the media? Does he play no role at all? Is he totally manipulated by the speaker, by the one who speaks on the radio, on television, in the newspapers? What do you think of free thinking? We have the impression that it no longer exists, if I follow you in your conclusions. People go one way or the other, depending on what they see in the media. What about their personal input? What is the place it takes?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I actually discuss this particular question when I talk about the two different frames that existed in the population for their beliefs and their -- their understanding of the relationship between Serbs and non-Serbs. And up to the time that the conflict becomes an armed conflict or up to the 1990 elections, when this nationalist propaganda really takes hold of -- of the politicians in the country, the -- the Yugoslav people outside of Kosovo -- and I cite surveys indicating -- big public opinion surveys which were done at this time in Yugoslavia, that indicated that most of the people believed that there were good and satisfactory relations between the -- between the different groups in their personal life, in their neighbourhoods, in the workplace, in civic activities, and so on. So that -- that's sort of the beliefs that they started with. Then I said there's a crisis discourse, which is based also on reality. It's based on the reality of the conflicts that took place in World War II and before that, World War I and the -- the Balkan wars, and in that discourse the people are afraid, fearful, feel threatened, have been victimised, and they interpret the political events that are explained -- that take place and that are explained to them by the political leaders in that frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One final example. Indeed, there's no end to this discussion. We saw a video-clip with a woman, a young woman going to war, it seemed. This young woman, her training, her education, what she learned in her past, if she learned that there were 500.000 or a million Serbs who were killed during World War II, one -- one person killed is one too many, but let -- if she had learned about those figures and she went to war in order to avoid that from being repeated, in her personal approach, which is the part of a decision made by a politician like Mr. Seselj? What is the determining factor? Is it her personal belief or what she may have heard from a politician?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's very much what she hears in the media, the -- what the -- what the public discourse becomes, what the politicians are saying. For 30 years and in the schools that she attended there wasn't any mention of 500.000 victims. All of this kind of history and material was very much not debated, suppressed during the Tito years, and it really didn't surface in a major way until the 1990 elections. So where did this lady and other people like that learn about these things? They learned it from this extreme nationalist political discourse that was taking place, especially in the 1990 election and afterwards. It wasn't something she carried out in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, but that's your belief.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that she learned it that way. But you're not in a position to prove this. This is a conclusion that you draw.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can I ...? I also cite several examples of interviews done by journalists with a -- a number of different Serbs and non-Serbs about why they were doing what they were doing. And let me ask you, in particular in one case that I cite here - and I could have cited many others - there's a woman who is a refugee with her family, a Serb woman who's a refugee from someplace in what became Republika Srpska, where she left her village to go to a -- another place where the Serbs are in the majority. And the journalist asks her, Why did you leave? And she said, "Because I heard on television that the Muslims are going to kill all the Serb men and all the women will become sex slaves of the -- of the Muslims in a harem to produce, you know, Muslim children." And, you know, she goes on and talks about what in fact was depicted on television and was part of the kind of xenophobic discourse. Then the journalist asks her, "Well, what about your neighbours," who were Muslim. And she says, "Well, they're fine people. I've lived with them in a friendly fashion all my life, but it's not my neighbours that I'm afraid of. It's those Muslims that they are talking about on television." And that just gives you a very vivid example - and I have other ones - of the impact that this kind of discourse has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. But this example of this woman who heard on television that she might be put in a harem, this woman might very well think that this is nonsense, gibberish said on television. Nothing forces her to go. So she does have a personal free will, in spite of the fact that she may have heard this on television. The fact that something is said on television doesn't mean that it is the truth. So in any decision, there must be a part of personal decision. There are other people than her who decided to stay. Mr. Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'll revert to what seems to me to be a discrepancy between your conclusion and your working thesis.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because what you told us a while ago was that the effects that you had been able to -- to establish of the accused's nationalist propaganda was the democratic conduct of the constituencies in the sense that before and after his speeches people changed their pattern of vote, democratic vote.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But how do you arrive from there to the, as you say, the coercion and violence by the Serbs against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are you assuming that because they changed their votes in exercising their democratic rights, they would also go out and -- and use violence against non-Serbs? Is that your thesis?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- well, let me say that in the beginning of my expert report I -- I do explain that the majority of the people who vote in a regime that creates and -- and advances a kind of an aggressive policy don't personally have to be in favour of any kind of armed violence or -- or killing, or anything like that. They just have to feel threatened and afraid and vote for politicians who then say, We will save you from this threat. Put your faith in us, and we will have a policy that will remove the threat. I also say in this early part - I think page 3 or 4, or something like that - that to execute this kind of aggressive policy, all you need is a fairly small number of people, maybe 5 to 10 per cent of the population, usually young males, who are either in the army or they're enlisted in paramilitaries or militias or maybe criminal bands, and, you know, in the -- in the -- in the case of -- in the case of Germany, they were the -- they were the -- the SS and the special troops and -- and you have these phenomenon in all of these, you know, armed conflicts. And the -- the crucial thing is you have a regime that produces a -- that pursues an aggressive policy against what they say is a threat. You have a majority of the voters who are persuaded that they're really doing a good thing by saving us. And you then you need about 10 per cent of really quite ordinary people who otherwise would not harm anybody in ordinary times, who are mobilised, armed, trained, and who then do the fighting. So you -- you don't have any kind of discourse that creates a bloodthirsty population out of a -- out of a normal population, but what you need is these three elements that come together. And they come together because political leaders and organisations want them to come together. And if they come together successfully, that's when you have the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But were you able to establish any such link between the accused's speeches and the factual commission of coercion or violence?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well -- no, I was -- what you have to do - and we tried to do it - that is, the Madam Prosecutor tried to do it by showing video-clips of -- like this lady in uniform getting on the bus, saying that she was alerted by what she saw on television about the dangers of the Serbs in Vukovar. We also had then a clip of the -- of the paramilitaries in uniform with their weapons who, when asked by the journalist, why they're there, they're pretty much repeating the kind of messages that -- that they picked up from this -- from this political discourse that I've -- that I've content analysed. And that's as far as we can go. No, there's no experimental evidence for -- in the same sense that we have it, you know, for the basic studies done about threat in a -- in an experimental setting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So what you are saying in your report is not that the accused's speeches actually did promote or justify a coercion of violence, but, rather, that in general terms it was conducive to such actions.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I -- I have a -- I have an example that I -- that you really ought to consider, because on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is it in your -- this --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in my report, and it corresponds to something said by one of these armed fighters in Vukovar as -- as to what he's doing and why he's doing it and why he's fighting there. And what he's saying is that the Croats have massacred all these small children in a school. That's what he's saying. That's why he's here, to prevent this massacre. Now, I quote the exact place and time that on -- on Serb TV there was a report by a journalist who quoted -- who said precisely that he had talked to people in Vukovar who had told him that there was this massacre of children at a school. I think he even mentions the number, 41. Now, the next day other people questioned this so-called fact and the journalist the next day retracted the story. It was a fabricated story. It was an untrue story. And -- and this is documented, and I refer to it. I wish -- you know, you will -- you will -- you will read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, this is a very good example where specifically we have a record of somebody who's armed, who's participating in the fighting, who says, The reason I came here is because of these children who were massacred. And then on television, before he came, there was this news story about the massacre, which was a total fabrication, as admitted by the TV station the next day. So that gives you an idea of what is happening here. Of course, the soldiers in the field didn't know this story was retracted and -- and generally speaking, a lot of falsehood was not really challenged and retracted at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sure that -- that in -- in science a lot of such examples can be mentioned, but just to be sure, this particular example that you mention was not in any way associated with the accused, was it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I'm concerned, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: One last question. You say that you have used what you call "content analysis."

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that to be a method of analysis?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- content analysis is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. That is a way of doing your analysis.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a quantitative way of analysing content, rather than -- based on large sets of records that are not arbitrarily selected to prove a point, and is different from the usual textual analysis, based on a few examples that one picks for a particular purpose. And that is content analysis. It was a technique developed after World War I and especially II in terms of analysing allied and Nazi propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What other methods could you have used, if any?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only thing I could have done is this -- which by the way, I would refuse to do, would be to pick and choose -- what's called cherry-picking, particular statements and kind of making a -- becoming an advocate for a -- for a certain point of view. I -- I told the Court that my method of content analysis is what is currently accepted in social science as the reliable and the most valid method, and I would not have used anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And you will assure us that it is not a qualitative method but purely a quantitative?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, all my coding that I did is indicated on every record. You can check for yourself. If you disagree with it, if you disagree with my coding, you can actually check what I have done and what you would do. So this is in the -- it's in the public domain. I have absolutely nothing to hide. And if anything, I would say that I gave Dr. Seselj the benefit of the doubt. When something wasn't clear, like he was making a sarcastic joke, and I said, Okay, this is his way of speaking to an audience; I didn't actually code that necessarily, because I took --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- you know, I took that into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, I only wanted to -- to be reassured that in your own understanding, you did not include any qualitative assessments in -- in your report. You -- you're basing this on a purely quantitative method that does not apply qualitative techniques.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I have to make a decision about what is victimhood and what is not victimhood. And if somebody says that genocide has been committed us -- against us in World War II, then, you know, that is victimhood. And the actual counts of the number of times this kind of victimhood is mentioned in all these texts is based on a -- on a count, which I also did. But if you disagree with my -- my view of victimhood and what I -- what I consider victimhood, it's all there for you to check, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Registrar, could I have two numbers for -- MFI numbers for Mr. Seselj's documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The article that the doctor referred -- Dr. Seselj referred to will be marked for identification as MFI D1, and the second rejoinder to the expert report will be marked for identification as MFI D2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mrs. Dahl, unless I'm wrong, did you ask for the report to be tendered? Yes. And did you get an MFI number?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: All of the documents have been marked for identification. There is a motion pending before the Chamber for admission of this material. Given that we are not trying to prove our entire case through one witness, that -- I renew the motion but consider it within the Chamber's discretion to decide when, at which point in time you receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The Trial Chamber will decide on this in due time. Mr. Oberschall, your testimony is now over. Thank you for coming here, and I wish you a safe trip home. Before adjourning, as you know, we will resume on Tuesday, January 8, 2008, and I believe that we will be sitting in the afternoon at 2.15. So see you then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of January, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.50 a.m.,
